abstract: Flatfishes exhibit the most extreme body asymmetry among vertebrates. During metamorphosis, one eye migrates across the dorsal midline of the skull, producing an adult that lies and swims on one side with both eyes on the upper side. Whether this body plan evolved once or repeatedly has been debated for over a century, with important implications for the evolution of the underlying developmental program. A recent genome-wide study supported multiple origins by placing Psettodes, the earliest-diverging flatfish, among symmetric relatives in Carangaria, the group that also includes billfishes, jacks, mahi-mahi, and barracudas. Later work traced that result to base-composition artifacts and inadequate substitution models. Here, we revisit the question using whole-genome phylogenomic and synteny data from 17 fish species. We add three new chromosome-level genome assemblies, including the first for Psettodes. Coalescent and other analyses of nucleotide data strongly support a single origin, with Psettodes placed as sister to other flatfishes. Microsynteny, measured from conserved gene-order blocks, supports the same result, whereas macrosynteny, based on chromosome-scale rearrangements, provides limited and reference-dependent support. This pattern likely reflects the different rates at which these changes accumulate. Gene-order rearrangements were frequent enough to resolve the short internodes of the rapid post-Cretaceous radiation of Carangaria, whereas chromosome-scale rearrangements accumulated too slowly to provide meaningful resolution. Together with shared developmental mechanisms and extensive fossil evidence, our results support a single origin of flatfish asymmetry, with gene order providing evidence independent of nucleotide substitution.
